TASK: CHECK EACH SENTENCE AGAINST THE CLAIMS

You are an adversarial fact checker. Your job is to find every sentence below that says something the CLAIMS do not support. Do not pass a sentence to be agreeable and do not fail one to look diligent. A sentence may read as confident or well written; that is evidence about its writer, not about the claims.

Label every sentence with exactly one of:
- "supported": every factual part of the sentence (each number, each name, each count, each comparison, each cause, each "most", "all", "only" or "none") is stated by one or more of the claims, or follows from them directly with no new number. Give the ids of the claims that together support it.
- "unsupported": any factual part is not stated by the claims, contradicts them, changes a number, drops a qualification a claim carries ("at most", "a bound", "notional", "not established", "candidate"), or states a number no claim states. Say which part, in the reason.
- "no_factual_content": the sentence states nothing that could be true or false about the world: a transition, a statement of what the section will do, a definition of a word the report uses.

The NAMES table maps a code in a claim to the name a sentence uses; a sentence that uses the name is read as if it used the code. A sentence that names a statistical body is checked against the claims for that body.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per sentence, in order, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:
[{"sentence_id": "S1", "label": "supported", "claim_ids": ["CL-035"], "reason": "one short sentence"}]

NAMES
B1: the check for variable-level semantics (Comprehensive variable-level metadata (labels, definitions, units, universes))
B4: the check for quality metadata (Data-quality attributes (error measures, suppression rules, revisions policy) published as metadata, not prose)
D3: the check for provenance completeness (Source lineage published (collection → processing → product))
D4: the check for no dark data (Statutory products enumerable from a public inventory (data.gov/agency inventory current))
G4: the check for authority metadata (The issuing authority of a data product is carried as machine-readable metadata on the product's catalog record: in `publisher`, the field DCAT-US 3.0 defines for it (Recommended), or in the agency codes DCAT-US 1.1 requires of federal datasets (`bureauCode`, `programCode`), which DCAT-US 3.0 does not define and does not reject)

[CL-079] (prior_art) A federal agency's flagship data product must be listed in its `data.json`.
    note: The status rests on the obligation covering every data asset, of which a flagship product is one. The statute and the guidance state the obligation for all data assets in the agency's possession; neither names flagship products. M-13-13 and the Project Open Data schema were not searched on the web: the current obligation (M-25-05, which names DCAT-US 3.0 as the inventory schema) is in the corpus, and the schema documents dcat-us-1-1-schema and dcat-us-3-overview are admitted.
    evidence: Evidence Act Title II, the amended 44 U.S.C. § 3511(a)(1), PDF p. 10 | quote: "develop and maintain a comprehensive data inventory that accounts for all data assets" | note: fss-policy-kg holds the same obligation: Obligation d7b0b83364ef4c66aa6e4718e267ca83 (source_doc evidence_act_2018) and 2346470a44d0415e855ad23ce5814085 (source_doc pra_1995_uslm).
    evidence: OMB M-25-05, comprehensive data inventories, (iii) Public Dissemination, PDF p. 10 | quote: "host it publicly on the agency’s website at the address: www.[agency].gov/data.json" | note: fss-policy-kg: Obligation 069f7c3081b64954b785c34ca1be3c22 (source_doc m_25_05); the inventory requirement itself is Obligation 7bf4bc7524e34df9bcdccac539f39ed3 (m_25_05, PDF p. 7: data assets held by more than one agency are 'required to be listed independently by each agency').

[CL-078] (prior_art) Structured metadata on a page does not by itself make data usable by machines; discovery, access, interpretation and fitness for use are each required.
    note: Corpus first: manifest title scan and MCP search_text ('fitness for use', 'machine-actionab'); both points are in admitted documents, so no web search was run. Not in the corpus and not searched on the web because the corpus establishes the point: Juran's 'fitness for use' (a book, no fetchable page carries the sentence); OMB's information quality guidelines (the corpus holds the statute, information-quality-act-data-quality-act-sec-515-of-p-l-106, not the guidelines).
    evidence: Wilkinson et al., Scientific Data 3:160018, PDF p. 3, the 'machine actionable' paragraph | quote: "but not capable of parsing it due to it being in an unknown format" | note: The FAIR paper's machine-actionability continuum: an agent must identify an object, judge it useful, judge it usable (licence, consent, access) and act; a machine can reach one step and fail the next.
    evidence: Wilkinson et al., Scientific Data 3:160018, PDF p. 3 | quote: "determine if it is usable, with respect to license, consent"
    evidence: FCSM 19-01, PDF p. 6 | quote: "data quality refers to the data’s “fitness for use” for a user’s own needs" | note: Federal statistical guidance on fitness for use; the same definition is in statistical-policy-working-paper-46-data-quality-assessment and w3c-dwbp-2017 §9 (MCP search_text 'fitness for use', six hits).

[CL-086] (prior_art) Data buried in aggregated spreadsheets is not machine-usable even when published.
    note: Neither source says 'not machine-usable' in those words: Wickham establishes presentation-layout tables as a common messy form that must be tidied before analysis, and the W3C Recommendation establishes that a format that is not machine-readable limits the data's usefulness. Corpus: DWBP admitted; Wickham not in the corpus (corpus grep 'Wickham', 'tidy data'). data.gov and Federal Data Strategy guidance were not searched: the task says one source suffices.
    evidence: Wickham, H. | 2014 | Tidy Data | §3.1 Column headers are values, not variable names | quote: "A common type of messy dataset is tabular data designed for presentation" | note: Read in the author's copy at the URL; the JSS abstract was confirmed at https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v059i10. §3 lists presentation layouts first among the five most common problems with messy datasets, each needing tidying before analysis.
    evidence: W3C Data on the Web Best Practices, Best Practice 12: Use machine-readable standardized data formats, Why | quote: "Posting data in a format that is not machine-readable places severe limitations" | note: The same paragraph separates formats humans can read and edit on a computer from formats that are machine-readable.

SENTENCES
S1: Where a host answered instead of refusing, the commonest outcome among the 1,055 findings was an absence, a case in which the item a check looked for was not served, and there are 415 of them.
S2: Against those, only 57 findings reach something present that falls short of the check, and 177 pass.
S3: The rest are the 341 refusals already described and 65 other errors of the kinds listed in the previous section.
S4: Absences weigh heavily because, as the opening section set out, use by a machine requires discovery, access, interpretation and fitness for use, each in its turn.
S5: Publication alone does not settle the matter either, because data buried in spreadsheets built for presentation is not usable by a machine even when it is published, as that section also noted.
S6: The Census Bureau shows how these results look for one publisher, since its published result tables mark 18 of 39 judged rows as failing.
S7: Those tables carry one row for each check and page they report, while the scan holds 89 findings for that publisher across every page it probed, so the tables show less than the full record.
S8: Every failing row falls on one of the two pages that present its flagship programs, the surveys and programs page and the American Community Survey page, and the same checks fail on both.
S9: The Census catalog also shows why something the scanner did not find must be kept apart from something that does not exist.
S10: The Census Bureau serves a catalog on census.gov holding 1,810 records, but no record in it names the products that were probed.
S11: Federal policy expects such a listing, because each agency must keep a public inventory of all its data assets on its own website, and a flagship product is one of those assets.
S12: Even so, the 20 Census findings that rest on that catalog, from the checks for variable-level semantics, quality metadata, provenance completeness, no dark data and authority metadata, are recorded as errors rather than failures.
S13: The reason is that the Commerce Department's inventory, which the check also names, refused the scanner, so although the Bureau's organization on catalog.data.gov was read, absence is not established.
S14: These findings therefore describe products absent from the catalogs that could be read, and they do not show that the Bureau left those products unlisted.
